Lakeview Family Medical Center - Discharge Summary
Patient: Maria Chen (fictional), 58-year-old adult
Discharge date: November 3, 2026
Attending: Dr. Helen Okafor, Family Medicine

Diagnosis:
Acute gout flare of the right big toe. This is your first gout flare.
Your uric acid level was 9.1 mg/dL. Your kidney blood test was normal.

Hospital course:
Fluid taken from the joint showed uric acid crystals and no infection.
Your pain improved with treatment and you are walking with mild discomfort.

Medications:
Colchicine 0.6 mg by mouth twice daily for 10 days.
Stop and call us if you have diarrhea.
Naproxen 500 mg by mouth every 12 hours as needed for pain.
Take with food.

Diet:
You should drink at least 2 liters of water a day.
Please avoid beer and liquor, and limit wine to one glass on any day.

Activity:
Rest and raise your right foot when you can for the next 3 days.

Follow-up:
See Dr. Helen Okafor on November 13, 2026 for a pain check.

Call 911 or return to the ER if:
- chest pain, trouble breathing, or fainting
- a fever of 101 F (38.3 C) or higher with chills

Call the clinic at 555-0142 if:
- your pain is not better after 3 days
- you have diarrhea, vomiting, or black stools

Riverside General Hospital - Discharge Summary
Patient: Robert Hale (fictional), 67-year-old adult
Discharge date: November 4, 2026
Attending: Dr. Marcus Bell, Internal Medicine

Diagnosis:
Acute gout flare of the left knee.
You also have chronic kidney disease, stage 3. Your creatinine was 1.8 mg/dL.
Your uric acid level was 8.7 mg/dL.

Hospital course:
Fluid taken from the knee showed uric acid crystals and no infection.
Your colchicine dose was lowered because of your kidneys.
The swelling in your knee has gone down.

Medications:
Colchicine 0.6 mg by mouth once daily for 7 days.
Stop and call us if you have diarrhea or muscle weakness.

Diet:
You should drink at least 1.5 liters of water a day unless the clinic tells you otherwise.
Please avoid beer and liquor.

Activity:
Rest your left knee and use a cane for the next 5 days.
Do not take over-the-counter anti-inflammatory pain pills without asking the clinic, because of your kidneys.

Follow-up:
See Dr. Marcus Bell on November 11, 2026 for a knee check.
See the clinic lab on November 18, 2026 for a kidney blood test.

Call 911 or return to the ER if:
- chest pain, trouble breathing, or fainting
- a fever of 101 F (38.3 C) or higher with chills

Call the clinic at 555-0142 if:
- your knee pain is not better after 3 days
- you have diarrhea, muscle weakness, or very little urine

Riverside General Hospital - Discharge Summary
Patient: Walter Brooks (fictional), 61-year-old adult
Discharge date: November 6, 2026
Attending: Dr. Marcus Bell, Internal Medicine

Diagnosis:
Acute gout flare of the left big toe.
Your uric acid level was 9.4 mg/dL. Your kidney blood test was normal.

Hospital course:
This is your third gout flare.
Your last flare in March 2026 improved within 3 days on prednisone, and you had no side effects.
You were treated with prednisone again and your pain has improved.

Medications:
Prednisone 30 mg by mouth once daily in the morning for 5 days.
Take with breakfast.

Your written flare plan:
At the first sign of a new flare, take prednisone 30 mg each morning for 5 days.
Call the clinic within 2 days of starting so we can check on you.
Keep a 5-day supply of prednisone at home.

Diet:
You should drink at least 2 liters of water a day.
Avoid sodas and juices sweetened with high-fructose corn syrup.

Activity:
Rest and raise your left foot when you can for the next 2 days.

Follow-up:
See Dr. Marcus Bell on November 20, 2026 to review your flare plan.

Call 911 or return to the ER if:
- chest pain, trouble breathing, or fainting
- a fever of 101 F (38.3 C) or higher with chills

Call the clinic at 555-0142 if:
- your pain is not better after 3 days
- you feel very thirsty or urinate much more than usual
